title: Logic Theorist and the General Problem Solver
text:
CHAPTER 9. SYMBOLIC AI
SECTION 9.1. LOGIC THEORIST AND THE GENERAL PROBLEM SOLVER

The first programs that most people agreed were doing something "intelligent" did not learn from data and did not imitate neurons. They manipulated symbols: logical formulas, goals and differences between states. Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw's Logic Theorist (1956) proved theorems from Principia Mathematica, and their General Problem Solver (from 1957) tried to capture a general method of human problem solving, means-ends analysis. These programs founded the symbolic tradition that dominated AI for about thirty years. This section explains how they worked, why heuristic search was the key idea, and what their limits taught the field.

1. The team

Allen Newell (1927-1992) was a researcher at the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, California, a think tank doing research for the US Air Force. Herbert A. Simon (1916-2001) was a political scientist and economist at the Carnegie Institute of Technology in Pittsburgh who studied decision making in organizations; he later received the 1978 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on decision-making processes, including the idea of "bounded rationality" (people "satisfice," seeking good-enough solutions, rather than optimizing). Cliff Shaw was a RAND systems programmer.

Newell was inspired in 1954 by a talk by Oliver Selfridge on pattern recognition, which convinced him that computers could do more than numerical calculation. He and Simon set out to simulate human thinking with programs. Simon later described the central idea: thinking is the manipulation of symbols, and a computer is a general-purpose symbol manipulator, so a computer can think. Newell and Simon shared the 1975 Turing Award for their contributions to AI, the psychology of human cognition and list processing.

2. The hand simulation

Before the program ran on a computer, it was simulated by people. In January 1956, Simon recalled, he gathered his wife, his three children and some graduate students; each was given 3 by 5 index cards containing one subroutine of the program, and when a "subroutine" was called, that person carried out the instructions on the card. So the family acted as the computer, a vivid demonstration that a program is a precise procedure independent of what executes it (the Turing view of Chapter 3). The same month Simon told a class that over Christmas he and Newell had "invented a thinking machine." Shaw then implemented the program, which ran on RAND's JOHNNIAC computer (a machine of the IAS design, named after John von Neumann) later in 1956.

3. Inventing list processing: IPL

Programs that manipulate formulas need flexible data structures: formulas are trees of varying size and shape, and the program must build, take apart and compare them. Machine languages of the time handled fixed arrays of numbers. Newell, Shaw and Simon invented the Information Processing Language (IPL) to solve this. IPL introduced:

  - linked lists: each cell holds a symbol and a pointer to the next cell, so structures can grow and shrink;
  - lists of lists, representing trees;
  - dynamic memory allocation from a pool of free cells;
  - recursion and stacks for subroutine calls.

These ideas became the basis of LISP (Section 9.2) and of essentially every data structures course since. List processing was arguably the most durable contribution of the Logic Theorist project.

4. What the Logic Theorist did

The Logic Theorist (LT) proved theorems in propositional logic from Chapter 2 of Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica (Section 1.2), starting from the book's five axioms and previously proven theorems. Principia's propositional theorems use "or" (v), "not" (~) and "implies" (->), for example:

    Theorem 2.01:  (p -> ~p) -> ~p
    Theorem 2.02:  q -> (p -> q)

LT worked backward from the theorem to be proved, looking for a chain of rules connecting it to axioms or known theorems. Its methods included:

  - Substitution: if the goal can be obtained from an axiom or known theorem by substituting expressions for variables (and replacing defined symbols by their definitions), the goal is proved.
  - Detachment (modus ponens used backward): to prove B, find a known theorem of the form A -> B, then set up A as a new subgoal.
  - Chaining (forward and backward): to prove A -> C, find a known theorem A -> B and set B -> C as a subgoal, or find B -> C and set A -> B as a subgoal, using transitivity of implication.

A small illustration of backward reasoning. Suppose the goal is p -> r, and the known theorems include p -> q and q -> r. Backward chaining from the goal p -> r: search for known theorems ending in "-> r"; find q -> r; create the subgoal p -> q; that matches a known theorem by substitution; done. The proof tree is built from the goal down to the known facts.

Results. LT proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in Chapter 2 of Principia. For Theorem 2.85 it found a proof that was shorter and more elegant than the one Whitehead and Russell had given. Newell, Simon and Shaw tried to publish the new proof, listing the Logic Theorist as a co-author, in The Journal of Symbolic Logic, but the paper was rejected on the grounds that a new proof of an elementary theorem was not notable.

5. Heuristic search: the key idea

The deepest point of LT was not logic but search. A brute-force method, sometimes called the "British Museum algorithm" in this literature, would generate all possible proofs in order of length and check each one. The number of possible proofs grows exponentially with length; for even modest theorems brute force is hopeless.

LT used heuristics to direct the search: ways of choosing which subgoals to pursue and which theorems to try, such as preferring subgoals that look similar to known theorems, and discarding subgoals that are too complex or that the program had good reason to believe were false (it checked candidate subgoals against simple counterexample tests). Heuristics do not guarantee finding a proof, but they find many proofs quickly.

In Newell and Simon's view, heuristic search was the central mechanism of intelligence: intelligent behavior is search through a space of possibilities, made feasible by knowledge that prunes and orders the search. The same idea appears in Samuel's checkers program (Section 8.3) and forms the basis of the search algorithms in Section 9.3.

Note how this contrasts with the 1936 results (Chapter 3). First-order logic is undecidable, and even propositional logic, though decidable, can need exponential time in the worst case. Heuristic search does not escape these limits; it bets that the problems people actually care about have structure that heuristics can exploit.

6. The General Problem Solver (GPS)

Encouraged by LT, Newell, Shaw and Simon built the General Problem Solver, starting in 1957 and described in papers around 1959. The aim was ambitious: to separate a general problem-solving method from the knowledge about any particular problem. GPS was implemented in IPL.

GPS represented a problem as:

  - objects: states of the world (for example, a logical expression, or the arrangement of disks in a puzzle);
  - operators: actions that transform one state into another, each with conditions under which it applies;
  - differences: ways in which the current state fails to match the goal;
  - a table of connections: for each type of difference, which operators are relevant to reducing it.

Means-ends analysis. GPS's central method alternated between three goal types:

  - Transform object A into object B: find a difference D between A and B. If none, done. Otherwise set up a subgoal to reduce D.
  - Reduce difference D between A and B: look up operators relevant to D and try one, Q.
  - Apply operator Q to A: if Q's conditions are not met by A, find the difference between A and Q's conditions and set up a subgoal to reduce it (recursion); then apply Q, producing A', and set up the goal to transform A' into B.

In plain pseudocode:

    function transform(A, B):
        D = most important difference between A and B
        if no difference: return success
        for each operator Q relevant to D (in order of preference):
            A1 = apply(Q, A)        -- may create subgoals
            if A1 succeeded and transform(A1, B) succeeds: return success
        return failure

    function apply(Q, A):
        if Q's preconditions hold in A: return result of Q on A
        C = Q's preconditions
        if transform(A, C) succeeds giving A2: return result of Q on A2
        return failure

An everyday illustration, paraphrasing a well-known example of this kind: I want to get my child to school. The difference is one of distance. What reduces distance? A car. The car will not start. What makes it start? A new battery. Where do I get a battery? A repair shop... Each step identifies a difference, an operator that reduces it, and a precondition that becomes a new subgoal.

GPS also ordered differences by importance, tackling the hardest ones first, and used the concept of planning in an abstracted problem space (ignoring minor differences) before filling in details.

GPS was applied to logic proofs, symbolic integration, the Towers of Hanoi puzzle, the "missionaries and cannibals" river-crossing puzzle, and other formal problems. Its operators and difference tables were supplied by people for each domain.

7. A worked example: Towers of Hanoi

The Towers of Hanoi has three pegs and n disks of decreasing size on the first peg. Goal: move all disks to the third peg, one at a time, never placing a larger disk on a smaller one. Means-ends reasoning finds the classic recursive solution:

  - The biggest difference: the largest disk is not on peg 3.
  - Operator: move the largest disk to peg 3. Precondition: no disks on top of it, and peg 3 empty (of smaller disks).
  - Subgoal: move the n - 1 smaller disks to peg 2 (out of the way). This is the same problem, one size smaller.
  - Then move the largest disk, then move the n - 1 disks from peg 2 to peg 3.

    hanoi(n, from, to, spare):
        if n == 0: return
        hanoi(n - 1, from, spare, to)
        move disk n from 'from' to 'to'
        hanoi(n - 1, spare, to, from)

The number of moves satisfies M(n) = 2 M(n - 1) + 1, M(0) = 0, so M(n) = 2^n - 1. For 3 disks, 7 moves; for 64 disks, about 1.8 * 10^19 moves. The puzzle is a good reminder that even a perfectly understood problem can be exponential.

8. Simulating human thought

Unlike many later AI researchers, Newell and Simon were explicitly trying to model human cognition, not just to get good performance. They compared GPS's traces with "think-aloud protocols," transcripts of people describing their reasoning while solving the same problems, and found similarities in the sequence of subgoals. This work helped found cognitive science and the information-processing approach to psychology. It culminated in their book "Human Problem Solving" (1972) and later in Newell's "unified theories of cognition" and the Soar architecture (1980s).

In their 1975 Turing Award lecture (published 1976), Newell and Simon stated the physical symbol system hypothesis: "A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action." In other words, intelligence just is the manipulation of symbol structures, and any system that is intelligent must be such a system. This hypothesis is the clearest statement of what symbolic AI believed. Connectionists (Chapter 13) and many later critics disputed it; modern neural networks process numbers, not explicit symbols, though they can learn to manipulate symbols.

9. Limits of GPS

GPS was "general" only in a restricted sense. Its problem-solving method was general, but:

  - Every domain required a human to supply the representation: states, operators, differences and the table of connections. The hard intellectual work of framing the problem was done by people.
  - On problems with large state spaces, search was easily lost in the combinatorial explosion.
  - It could not handle the messy, open-ended problems of the real world, where the relevant objects, operators and differences are not given.

Work on GPS continued into the 1960s before the project was set aside. Its successor ideas, however, were widely used: means-ends analysis became a standard technique, the separation of general inference methods from domain knowledge shaped later systems, and the STRIPS planner (1971), developed at SRI for the Shakey robot (Section 9.4), described actions by preconditions and effects in a direct descendant of GPS's operator idea. STRIPS-style action models are still used in automated planning and robotics.

The lesson that the field eventually drew was that general methods are weak without large amounts of domain knowledge. That conclusion led, in the late 1960s and 1970s, to the knowledge-based approach and expert systems (Chapter 12), the "knowledge is power" reaction against the search for a universal problem solver.

10. Summary

  - Newell (RAND), Simon (Carnegie Tech) and Shaw (RAND) built the Logic Theorist in 1955-1956; it was hand-simulated with index cards in January 1956 and then ran on the JOHNNIAC.
  - They invented IPL, introducing linked lists, dynamic allocation and recursive list processing.
  - LT proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in Chapter 2 of Principia Mathematica using substitution, detachment and chaining in backward search, finding a more elegant proof of Theorem 2.85.
  - Its key idea was heuristic search: guiding search with rules of thumb instead of brute-force enumeration.
  - GPS (from 1957) implemented means-ends analysis: find differences between current state and goal, apply operators that reduce them, and recursively achieve operator preconditions.
  - Newell and Simon modeled human thinking, won the 1975 Turing Award, and stated the physical symbol system hypothesis; GPS's limits pointed the field toward domain knowledge and expert systems.
